mainTopic: Words that make an oath or curse (אלה, ארור, אמן, 'no'/'yes'), cursing with ה׳'s names, and whether רבי מאיר infers a 'yes' from a 'no'
overview: This amud continues the topic of putting witnesses under oath (שבועת העדות). It first learns that an אלה alone or a שבועה alone is enough, and it proves that אלה means an oath. Next it shows that the word ארור has three meanings: נידוי, קללה and שבועה. Along the way it uses the missing 'ו' in 'ארור' to answer a challenge. רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא teaches the three meanings of אמן. Then רבי אלעזר and רבא teach that 'no, no' or 'yes, yes' can be an oath. Back in the משנה, רבי מאיר and the חכמים argue about cursing ה׳ or parents with a כינוי, and everyone agrees that cursing oneself or another person is forbidden. Two stories teach that one should reword a curse so it does not sound aimed at one's teacher, even when quoting a פסוק. Finally, the גמרא asks how רבי מאיר can infer a 'yes' from a 'no' when a witness is told 'may God bless you'. It answers that the difference is money matters versus איסור matters, and then challenges that answer from סוטה. The challenge continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Does a curse alone or an oath alone count?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks where we learn that an אלה without the word שבועה, and a שבועה without the word אלה, count just like when both words are used.
steps.simpleTranslation: From where do we learn that an אלה said without the word שבועה is just like an אלה said with it, and a שבועה said without the word אלה is just like a שבועה said with it?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא asks a question about how witnesses are put under oath. It is setting up the next step, where a פסוק gives the answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The case of witnesses in the תורה mentions an אלה, and oaths often use both words together. So the question is whether each word works alone. If one word works by itself, the witnesses can still be liable even if the other word was never said.

keyTerms.meaning: A curse-oath, an oath said with a curse

phrases.english: And from where do we learn to treat an ala
that has no oath with it
like an ala that has an oath with it,
and an oath that has no ala with it
phrases.notes: He means the word itself: someone said only 'שבועה' and never said 'אלה'.

phrases.english: like an oath that has an ala with it?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִנַּיִן לַעֲשׂוֹת אָלָה שֶׁאֵין עִמָּהּ שְׁבוּעָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the earlier discussion of how witnesses are put under oath, now asking for a source.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source showing that אלה alone and שבועה alone each count for שבועת העדות.

steps.title: The verse splits 'voice of an אלה' into two
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא answers from 'ושמעה קול אלה', reading it as two separate things: hearing an אלה, and hearing a קול.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says: 'And he hears the voice of an אלה.' Read it as: he heard an אלה, or he heard a voice.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers the question from step 1 using the words of the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase 'קול אלה' is read as two parts, and each part works by itself. So an אלה alone makes the witnesses liable, and a קול (a spoken oath) alone does too. You do not need both words together.

keyTerms.meaning: The verse teaches, the פסוק says
'And he hears the voice of an אלה', the פסוק about witnesses
A voice; here, a spoken oath

steps.whatToRemember: For witnesses, an אלה alone or a שבועה alone is enough. The two words do not have to be said together.

phrases.english: The verse states:
"And he hears the voice of an ala" –
phrases.notes: ויקרא 5:1

phrases.english: he heard an ala, and he heard a voice.
phrases.notes: The גמרא splits the phrase in two, so each part counts by itself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 1.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק is read as 'he heard an אלה' and 'he heard a voice', so each one works alone.

steps.title: Proof that אלה means an oath
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו proves that אלה means a שבועה by matching a פסוק in יחזקאל with a פסוק in דברי הימים about the same event.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבהו said: From where do we know that אלה is an oath? From the פסוק 'and he brought him into an אלה', together with the פסוק 'and he also rebelled against King נבוכדנצר, who had made him swear by God.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבהו gives a source that the word אלה means a real oath.
steps.deeperAnalysis: יחזקאל describes the king of בבל bringing a member of the royal family 'into an אלה'. דברי הימים describes the same thing with צדקיהו and says נבוכדנצר 'made him swear'. Since both פסוקים describe one event, the אלה in one is the oath in the other.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows why an אלה can count as an oath in שבועת העדות at all.

phrases.english: Rabbi Abbahu says:
From where do we know that "ala" is an oath?
As it is stated: "And he brought him into an ala, etc.";
phrases.notes: יחזקאל 17:13

phrases.english: and it is written:
"And he also rebelled against King Nebuchadnezzar
who had made him swear by God."
phrases.notes: דברי הימים ב 36:13. It describes the same event, so that אלה was an oath.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ: מִנַּיִן לְ״אָלָה״ שֶׁהִיא שְׁבוּעָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After step 2 said that an אלה alone counts, this step proves that אלה really is an oath.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The word אלה means a שבועה, as shown by comparing the two פסוקים about צדקיהו.

steps.title: The word ארור has three meanings
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that the word ארור includes three ideas: נידוי, קללה, and שבועה.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: the word ארור has a ban in it, a curse in it, and an oath in it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that defines a related word, ארור. This sets up the next steps, which prove each of the three meanings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like אלה, the word ארור is not just one thing. The ברייתא lists three meanings, and the גמרא will now find a פסוק for each one, starting with נידוי.

keyTerms.meaning: A ban; pushing someone out of the community

phrases.english: It was taught: "Arur" –
there is ostracism in it,
there is a curse in it, there is an oath in it.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנָא: ״אָרוּר״ – בּוֹ נִידּוּי, בּוֹ קְלָלָה, בּוֹ שְׁבוּעָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from defining אלה to defining the related word ארור.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ארור carries three meanings: נידוי, קללה, and שבועה.

steps.title: ארור means a ban: the story of מרוז
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא proves that ארור includes נידוי from the curse on מרוז in שירת דבורה, along with עולא's teaching that ברק banned מרוז with 400 שופר blasts.
steps.simpleTranslation: It has a ban in it, as it is written: 'Curse מרוז, said the angel of ה׳, curse bitterly its inhabitants.' And עולא said: ברק placed מרוז under a ban with four hundred שופר blasts.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proves the first of the three meanings from step 4, that ארור includes נידוי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק uses the word ארור for מרוז. עולא teaches that what actually happened was that ברק placed מרוז under a ban, a שמתא, with שופר blasts. So the word ארור there means a ban.

keyTerms.meaning: A city cursed in שירת דבורה
He placed it under a ban (שמתא)
The general who fought with דבורה

phrases.english: There is ostracism in it – as it is written:
"Curse Meroz, said the angel of the Lord,
phrases.notes: שופטים 5:23

phrases.english: curse bitterly its inhabitants",
and Ulla says:
With four hundred shofar blasts
Barak placed Meroz under a ban.
phrases.notes: שמתא is a ban, so this ties the word ארור to נידוי.

steps.triggerLanguage: בּוֹ נִידּוּי – דִּכְתִיב: ״אוֹרוּ מֵרוֹז אָמַר מַלְאַךְ ה׳
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Proves the first meaning, נידוי, from the list in step 4.
steps.raayaObject: That the word ארור includes נידוי.
steps.raayaSupportSource: שופטים 5:23 (the curse on מרוז), together with עולא's teaching that ברק banned מרוז with 400 שופר blasts.

steps.title: Proof that ארור includes a curse
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא proves that ארור includes קללה from the ceremony at הר גריזים and הר עיבל, where the 'curse' section is filled with sentences that begin with ארור.
steps.simpleTranslation: ארור includes a curse, because the תורה says 'these shall stand for the curse,' and then the curses are spelled out as 'ארור is the man who makes an idol.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now proves the second of the three ideas in ארור: that it is a קללה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תורה calls one part of the ceremony 'the curse,' and the sentences said in that part start with ארור. So ארור is the language of a curse. This proof goes through without any challenge.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And so on.' The rest of the פסוק is not quoted

phrases.english: It includes a curse
as it is written: 'And these shall stand for the curse,'
phrases.notes: דברים 27:13

phrases.english: and it is written: 'Cursed is the man'
who makes a carved idol, and so on.'
phrases.notes: דברים 27:15

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After proving נידוי in step 5, the גמרא moves to the second idea, קללה.
steps.raayaObject: That the word ארור carries the meaning of קללה.
steps.raayaSupportSource: דברים 27:13 together with 27:15: the 'curse' section is made up of ארור sentences.

steps.title: First attempt to prove that ארור includes an oath
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tries to prove that ארור includes a שבועה from יהושע, who 'made them swear' by saying 'ארור is the man who rebuilds יריחו.'
steps.simpleTranslation: ארור includes an oath, because the פסוק says 'יהושע made them swear at that time, saying: ארור is the man before ה׳ who rebuilds this city.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now tries to prove the third idea in ארור, that it is a שבועה. It uses the story of יהושע and יריחו.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק calls what יהושע did an oath ('וישבע'), and the words of that oath are 'ארור.' So it seems that saying ארור is a way of making an oath. The next step will question this proof.

keyTerms.meaning: יהושע, who led the people after משה

phrases.english: It includes an oath
as it is written: 'And יהושע made them swear at that time, saying:'
phrases.notes: יהושע 6:26

phrases.english: 'Cursed is the man before ה׳, and so on.'
phrases.notes: The rest of the פסוק is about anyone who rebuilds יריחו.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the third idea of ארור, שבועה.
steps.raayaObject: That the word ארור carries the meaning of שבועה.

steps.title: Maybe יהושע did two separate things
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the proof: maybe יהושע both made them swear and also cursed them, so ארור is only the curse part.
steps.simpleTranslation: But maybe יהושע did two things to them: he made them swear, and he cursed them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pokes a hole in the proof from יהושע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof only works if ארור is the actual wording of the oath. But perhaps the oath was one act and the ארור was a second, separate curse. If so, ארור would only mean a curse, not an oath.

phrases.english: But perhaps he did two things to them:
he made them swear, and he cursed them?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the proof in step 7.
steps.kashyaTarget: The proof from יהושע that ארור means שבועה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The oath and the curse might be two separate acts, so ארור could be only the curse.

steps.title: New proof of the oath from שאול
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a new proof: שאול 'put the people under an oath' by saying 'ארור is the man who eats,' and later the פסוק calls this an oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, learn it from here: 'שאול put the people under an oath, saying: ארור is the man who eats bread before evening.' And later it says: 'יהונתן did not hear when his father made the people swear.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops the יהושע proof and brings a different one, from שאול during the war with the פלשתים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here two פסוקים work together. The first gives שאול's words, 'ארור is the man who eats.' The second calls that same event 'בהשביע,' making the people swear. So the ארור statement is called an oath.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Rather, from here.' A new source replaces the old one
'He put under an oath.' It comes from the word אָלָה
שאול, the first king of Israel

phrases.english: Rather, learn it from here:
'And the men of Israel were hard-pressed that day,'
phrases.notes: שמואל א 14:24

phrases.english: 'and שאול put the people under an oath, saying:'
phrases.notes: ויואל comes from אלה. Step 3 showed that אלה means an oath.

phrases.english: 'Cursed is the man who eats, and so on.'
And it is written: 'But יהונתן did not hear'
'when his father made the people swear.'
phrases.notes: שמואל א 14:27

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Because of the challenge in step 8, the גמרא replaces the יהושע proof with one from שאול.
steps.raayaSupportSource: שמואל א 14:24 and 14:27, where the ארור statement is called 'בהשביע.'

steps.title: The same challenge against the proof from שאול
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks the same question again: maybe שאול also did two separate things, an oath and a curse.
steps.simpleTranslation: But perhaps here too he did two things to them: he made them swear, and he cursed them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא aims the same challenge from step 8 at the new proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if the event is called an oath, the ארור might be a separate curse added next to the oath. So the new proof seems to have the same weakness as the old one.

phrases.english: But perhaps here too
he did two things to them:
he made them swear, and he cursed them?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְדִלְמָא הָכָא נָמֵי תַּרְתֵּי עֲבַד לְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Repeats the challenge of step 8 against the proof in step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: The proof from שאול that ארור means שבועה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The oath and the curse may still be two separate acts.

steps.title: The פסוק does not say 'and cursed'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the פסוק does not say 'וארור' ('and cursed'), so ארור is not a second act. It is the wording of the oath itself.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does it say 'and cursed'?! (No. So ארור is the oath itself.)
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by looking closely at how the פסוק is worded.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If שאול had done two separate things, the פסוק would say 'he made them swear, and cursed...' with an 'and' (ו). Since it says 'saying: ארור,' the word ארור is simply what he said when he made them swear. So ארור is the wording of the oath.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Is it written?!' A strong way of saying it is not written
'And cursed.' With the letter ו, it would mean a separate, added act

steps.confusionAlert: The whole answer depends on one letter, the ו. 'ארור' with no ו is the content of the oath. 'וארור' would have meant a second, separate curse.

phrases.english: Is it written 'and cursed'?!
phrases.notes: It says only 'ארור' with no 'and,' so the curse is the words of the oath, not something extra.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Close reading of the wording (no ו connecting the oath and the curse)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: שאול might have made an oath and also added a separate curse.
steps.terutzMaskana: Since the פסוק does not say 'וארור,' the ארור is the oath itself, so ארור means שבועה.

steps.title: The same answer saves the proof from יהושע
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that the יהושע פסוק also does not say 'וארור,' so the first proof works after all.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now that you have reached this point, there too (by יהושע) it does not say 'and cursed.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the first proof from יהושע and shows that the same answer fixes it too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge in step 8 is answered the same way as step 10. The יהושע פסוק says 'וישבע... לאמר ארור' with no ו. So both פסוקים show that ארור is a form of שבועה.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Now that you have reached this.' Using a new idea to look back at something earlier
'There.' Here it means the יהושע פסוק

steps.whatToRemember: ארור includes three ideas: נידוי (from מרוז), קללה (from הר עיבל), and שבועה (from יהושע and שאול). The proof for שבועה rests on the fact that the פסוקים say 'ארור' and not 'וארור.'
steps.whyThisMatters: Since ארור counts as an oath, someone who puts witnesses under an oath using the word ארור has made a real שבועה.

phrases.english: Now that you have come to this,
there too it is not written 'and cursed.'
phrases.notes: 'There' means the פסוק about יהושע from step 7.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the answer from step 11 to bring back the proof from step 7.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Both the יהושע פסוק and the שאול פסוק prove that ארור is a שבועה, because neither one says 'וארור.'

steps.title: The word אמן has three meanings
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא teaches that אמן can mean an oath, an acceptance of what was said, or a confirmation of what was said.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא said: The word 'אמן' has three things inside it: an oath, accepting what was said, and confirming what was said.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new teaching from רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא listing three meanings of the word אמן. This sets up the next three steps, where each meaning gets its own source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the סוגיא asked whether ארור can serve as an oath. Now the focus moves to אמן. The teaching says אמן is not one fixed thing: depending on the setting, it can be a שבועה, a קבלת דברים, or a האמנת דברים.

keyTerms.meaning: Amen; a word said in response to someone else's words
Accepting the words; agreeing to take on what was said
Confirming the words; affirming them and wishing that they should come true

steps.confusionAlert: The word בּוֹ here means 'in it', referring to the word אמן. It does not mean 'with him'. Each meaning is something that can be contained inside the word אמן.
steps.whyThisMatters: This explains how answering אמן to someone else's oath can make it as if the person himself swore. It also shows that אמן can mean other things too.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Chanina, said:
"Amen": there is an oath in it,
there is acceptance of the words in it,
there is confirmation of the words in it.
phrases.notes: He means agreeing that what was said is true, and hoping it will happen.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא: אָמֵן בּוֹ שְׁבוּעָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The ארור discussion is finished. This opens a new teaching about the meanings of אמן.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אמן can carry three meanings: oath, acceptance of words, and confirmation of words.

steps.title: Source that אמן can be an oath
steps.stepSummary: The סוטה woman answers 'אמן אמן' to the כהן's oath, which shows that אמן can work as a שבועה.
steps.simpleTranslation: It has an oath in it, as it is written: 'And the woman shall say: Amen, Amen.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a פסוק to prove the first meaning: that אמן can be an oath.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the סוטה procedure the כהן says the oath, and the woman only answers אמן. Her אמן is what makes her part of the oath. So answering אמן is the same as swearing.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is written; introduces a פסוק
The woman; here the סוטה, the woman suspected by her husband

phrases.english: There is an oath in it, as it is written:
"And the woman shall say: Amen, Amen."
phrases.notes: במדבר 5:22. Just before this, the כהן makes her swear, and her 'Amen' is her answer.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a source for the first of the three meanings listed in step 13.
steps.raayaObject: That אמן can function as a שבועה.
steps.raayaSupportSource: במדבר 5:22: the סוטה answers 'אמן אמן' to the כהן's oath.

steps.title: Source that אמן can mean accepting what was said
steps.stepSummary: At הר עיבל the people answered אמן to 'Cursed is the one who does not uphold this Torah', which shows that they accepted it on themselves.
steps.simpleTranslation: It has acceptance of the words in it, as it is written: 'Cursed is the one who will not uphold the words of this Torah to do them, and all the people shall say: Amen.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a פסוק to prove the second meaning: that אמן can mean accepting something on yourself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the people say אמן here, they are not just saying the curse is true. They are agreeing to take on the words of the תורה and keep them. That is קבלת דברים.

phrases.english: There is acceptance of the words in it, as it is written:
"Cursed is the one who will not uphold

phrases.aramaic: אֶת דִּבְרֵי הַתּוֹרָה הַזֹּאת לַעֲשׂוֹת אוֹתָם,
phrases.english: the words of this Torah, to do them,
and all the people shall say: Amen."
phrases.notes: דברים 27:26

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a source for the second of the three meanings listed in step 13.
steps.raayaObject: That אמן can mean קבלת דברים, accepting what was said.
steps.raayaSupportSource: דברים 27:26: the people answer אמן, taking the Torah on themselves.

steps.title: Source that אמן can mean confirming and wishing it comes true
steps.stepSummary: ירמיה answered 'אמן, so may ה׳ do' to חנניה's words, which shows that אמן can be a wish that the words come true.
steps.simpleTranslation: It has confirmation of the words in it, as it is written: 'And ירמיה the prophet said: Amen, so may ה׳ do; may ה׳ fulfill your words.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a פסוק to prove the third meaning: that אמן can mean 'may it come true'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ירמיה is not swearing here, and he is not taking anything on himself. His אמן is followed by 'so may ה׳ do', so it is a hope that what was said will come true. That is האמנת דברים.

keyTerms.meaning: חנניה, the person ירמיה was answering
May He fulfill, may He establish

steps.whatToRemember: אמן has three meanings. (1) An oath: the סוטה says אמן to the כהן's oath. (2) Acceptance: the people say אמן to keeping the תורה. (3) Confirmation, meaning 'may it come true': ירמיה says 'אמן, so may ה׳ do'.

phrases.english: There is confirmation of the words in it, as it is written:
"And Jeremiah [the prophet] said (to Hananiah),
phrases.notes: Some versions have the words in round brackets and some don't; the word in square brackets is the corrected wording, which matches the פסוק.

phrases.english: Amen, so may the Lord do;
may the Lord fulfill your words."
phrases.notes: ירמיהו 28:6

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a source for the third and last meaning listed in step 13, which completes the teaching.
steps.raayaObject: That אמן can mean האמנת דברים, confirming the words and wishing that they come true.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ירמיהו 28:6: 'אמן, so may ה׳ do; may ה׳ fulfill your words.'

steps.title: A plain 'no' or 'yes' can be an oath
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר teaches that saying 'no' or 'yes' can work as a שבועה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר said: 'No' is an oath, and 'yes' is an oath.
steps.whatsHappening: Right after the teaching about אמן, the גמרא brings another simple word that can work as a שבועה. רבי אלעזר says 'no' and 'yes' can count as an oath.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The steps before showed that אמן can be a שבועה. Now רבי אלעזר adds two more everyday words, לאו and הן. The next steps will ask where each of these comes from.

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar said:
"No" is an oath,
"Yes" is an oath.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds two more words, after אמן, that can act as a שבועה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Saying 'no' or 'yes' can count as a שבועה.

steps.title: Proof that 'no' is an oath from the flood
steps.stepSummary: ה׳ said the flood would 'not' come again, and נביא ישעיה calls that promise a שבועה.
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense that 'no' is an oath, because it says 'And the waters shall no more become a flood,' and it says 'For this is as the waters of נח to Me, that I swore.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proves the 'no' half of רבי אלעזר's teaching. ה׳ promised with a 'no' that there would be no more flood, and a later פסוק calls that promise an oath.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In בראשית the promise is only worded as 'there will not be.' In ישעיה the same promise is described as 'I swore.' So a 'no' statement counted as a שבועה. The word בשלמא tells us this half is easy, and the hard question about 'yes' is coming next.

keyTerms.meaning: It makes sense / granted (this part is fine)
The flood in the time of נח

phrases.english: It makes sense that "no" is an oath,
as it is written: "And the waters shall no more become a flood,"
phrases.notes: בראשית 9:15

phrases.english: and it is written: "For this is as the waters of Noah to Me,
that I swore."
phrases.notes: ישעיה 54:9. The 'no' promise from בראשית is called an oath here.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for the first half of רבי אלעזר's statement.

steps.title: Where do we learn that 'yes' is an oath?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for a source for the 'yes' half of רבי אלעזר's teaching.
steps.simpleTranslation: But that 'yes' is an oath, from where do we know it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets up its next move. The 'no' part has a פסוק, but no פסוק has been shown for 'yes'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The flood פסוקים only show a 'no' promise. So the 'yes' part still needs a source.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do we know this?

phrases.english: But that "yes" is an oath, from where do we know it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Points out that the proof only covered 'no'.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source showing that 'yes' can be a שבועה.

steps.title: 'Yes' is learned from logic
steps.stepSummary: Since 'no' works as an oath, it is logical that 'yes' does too.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is logic: since 'no' is an oath, 'yes' is also an oath.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that no פסוק is needed for 'yes'. Plain reasoning tells us it works just like 'no'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A 'no' and a 'yes' are two sides of the same kind of firm statement. If one can be an oath, there is no reason the other cannot.

phrases.english: It is logic:
since "no" is an oath,
"yes" is also an oath.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about 'yes'.

steps.title: Only when said twice
steps.stepSummary: רבא limits רבי אלעזר's rule: 'no' or 'yes' is an oath only when said two times.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: That is only when he said 'no, no' two times, or 'yes, yes' two times.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא adds a condition to רבי אלעזר's rule. A single 'no' or 'yes' is not enough; it must be said twice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעזר did not say how many times the word must be said. רבא narrows it down: only a doubled 'no, no' or 'yes, yes' counts as a שבועה.
steps.confusionAlert: רבא is not arguing with רבי אלעזר. He agrees that 'no' and 'yes' can be an oath, and only adds that the word must be said twice.

phrases.english: Rava said:
And that is only when he said "no, no" two times,
or when he said "yes, yes" two times;

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a condition to רבי אלעזר's rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'No' or 'yes' is a שבועה only when said twice.

steps.title: The flood promise said 'no' twice
steps.stepSummary: ה׳'s promise about the flood used 'not' two times, and 'yes' follows the same rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it says, 'And all flesh shall not be cut off any more by the waters of the flood,' and 'And the waters shall no more become a flood.' Since 'no' was said twice, 'yes' too must be said twice.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings רבא's source. The flood promise that was called an oath has two 'no' statements, so an oath of 'no' needs two.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'no' oath at the flood is said in two separate פסוקים. That shows the oath came from saying it twice. Just as 'yes' was learned from 'no' before, it also copies this twice rule.
steps.whatToRemember: A 'no' or 'yes' counts as a שבועה (רבי אלעזר), but only when said twice, like 'no, no' (רבא). The rules for 'no' come from the flood promise, and 'yes' follows 'no' by logic.

phrases.english: as it is written: "And all flesh shall not be cut off
any more by the waters of the flood,"
phrases.notes: בראשית 9:11. This is the first 'no'; the next פסוק is the second.

phrases.english: and "And the waters shall no more become a flood";
and since "no" needs two times,
"yes" also needs two times.

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּכְתִיב: ״וְלֹא יִכָּרֵת כׇּל בָּשָׂר עוֹד מִמֵּי הַמַּבּוּל״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for רבא's twice rule.
steps.raayaObject: That 'no' and 'yes' are an oath only when said twice.
steps.raayaSupportSource: בראשית 9:11 and 9:15, two 'no' statements about the flood.

steps.title: Back to the משנה: cursing with any of the names
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה: רבי מאיר makes one who curses with any of ה׳'s names liable, and the חכמים exempt him.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who curses with any of them is liable; these are the words of רבי מאיר. And the חכמים exempt him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new line of the משנה. This sets up the ברייתא that will explain the מחלוקת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה listed names and descriptive names of ה׳. רבי מאיר says cursing with any of them makes a person liable. The חכמים say he is exempt, and the ברייתא will show what exactly they mean.

phrases.english: One who curses with any of them is liable,
phrases.notes: 'Them' means all the names and descriptive names of ה׳ listed in the משנה.

phrases.english: these are the words of Rabbi Meir,
and the Rabbis exempt him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic from the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי מאיר: liable for cursing with any of the names. חכמים: exempt.

steps.title: Why does the Torah need a second פסוק about cursing?
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא asks why the Torah needs 'איש איש כי יקלל אלהיו' when it already says 'ונקב שם ה׳ מות יומת'.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: 'Any man who curses his God shall bear his sin.' Why does the פסוק need to say this? Doesn't it already say 'And one who curses the name of ה׳ shall be put to death'?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא asks why there is an extra פסוק about cursing ה׳. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The next פסוק already gives the death penalty for cursing ה׳'s name. So the earlier פסוק looks extra, and the ברייתא expects it to teach something new.

keyTerms.meaning: Why does the פסוק need to say this?
Curses, says the name in a curse

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
"Any man who curses his God
phrases.notes: ויקרא 24:15. The word in square brackets is added so the פסוק reads correctly: 'איש איש'.

phrases.english: shall bear his sin."
Why does the verse need to say this?
Wasn't it already said:
"And one who curses the name of the Lord shall be put to death"!
phrases.notes: ויקרא 24:16

steps.triggerLanguage: מָה תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר? וַהֲלֹא כְּבָר נֶאֱמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins the ברייתא that explains the משנה's מחלוקת.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the extra פסוק 'איש איש כי יקלל אלהיו' comes to teach.

steps.title: רבי מאיר: the extra פסוק includes the כינויים
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר says the extra פסוק makes one liable even for cursing with a כינוי, not only the שם המיוחד.
steps.simpleTranslation: I might think he is liable only for the special name of ה׳. From where do we include the descriptive names? The פסוק says 'Any man who curses his God': in any case. These are the words of רבי מאיר.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers that the extra פסוק teaches liability for cursing with ה׳'s descriptive names too. This is רבי מאיר's view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without this פסוק we would think only the שם המיוחד counts. The word 'אלהיו' (his God), with the doubled 'איש איש', teaches 'in any case,' so the כינויים are included. That is why רבי מאיר in the משנה says the curser is liable with any of the names.

keyTerms.meaning: ה׳'s special name, the four-letter name

phrases.english: I might think he would be liable
only for the special name of God alone;
from where do we include the descriptive names?
The verse says:
"Any man who curses his God," etc.:
in any case.
These are the words of Rabbi Meir.

steps.triggerLanguage: יָכוֹל לֹא יְהֵא חַיָּיב אֶלָּא עַל שֵׁם הַמְיוּחָד בִּלְבַד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers why the extra פסוק is needed.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The extra פסוק includes the כינויים, according to רבי מאיר.

steps.title: חכמים: death for the special name, a prohibition for the כינויים
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים say cursing the שם המיוחד carries death, while cursing a כינוי is only an אזהרה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים say: for the special name, death; and for the descriptive names, a prohibition.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives the view of the חכמים. They agree that cursing with a כינוי is forbidden, but it does not carry the death penalty.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This explains what 'exempt' in the משנה means. The חכמים do not allow cursing with a כינוי. They only exempt the person from מיתה, since the death penalty is limited to the שם המיוחד.

keyTerms.meaning: Death penalty given by בית דין
A warning, a prohibition without death

steps.confusionAlert: 'The חכמים exempt him' does not mean cursing with a כינוי is allowed. It is still forbidden; he is only exempt from the death penalty.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי מאיר: cursing ה׳ even with a כינוי carries death. חכמים: death only for the שם המיוחד; a כינוי is an אזהרה.

phrases.english: And the Rabbis say:
for the special name, it is with death;
and for the descriptive names, it is with a prohibition.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the חכמים's view, opposite רבי מאיר's.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Death penalty only for cursing with the שם המיוחד; cursing with a כינוי is an אזהרה only.

steps.title: Who are the חכמים in the case of cursing parents?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about cursing one's father and mother and asks which תנא is the 'חכמים' who exempt him.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'One who curses his father and mother, etc.' Who are these חכמים?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next line of the משנה, about cursing parents with ה׳'s names, and asks who the חכמים there are. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said רבי מאיר makes him liable even for a כינוי, and the חכמים exempt him. The גמרא wants a named source for the חכמים' view, so we know where their rule comes from.

keyTerms.meaning: One who curses his father and mother
Who are the חכמים? (which תנא holds this view)

phrases.english: And one who curses his father and his mother, etc.
phrases.notes: This quotes the משנה: רבי מאיר makes him liable even with a כינוי, and the חכמים exempt him.

phrases.english: Who are the חכמים?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from cursing ה׳ to the next case in the משנה, cursing parents.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The identity of the תנא behind the חכמים' opinion that one who curses parents with a כינוי is exempt.

steps.title: It is רבי מנחם בר יוסי, who learns it from the word 'שם'
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים are רבי מנחם בר יוסי, who learns from the extra word 'שם' that one who curses his parents is only liable if he uses the שם המיוחד.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is רבי מנחם בר יוסי. A ברייתא teaches that he said: the פסוק says 'when he curses a name, he shall be put to death.' Why does it need to say 'name'? To teach that one who curses his father and mother is not liable unless he curses them with the שם.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the חכמים are רבי מנחם בר יוסי. It brings his ברייתא, which uses an extra word in the פסוק to teach the rule for cursing parents.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק about cursing ה׳ already said 'ונוקב שם ה׳', so the second 'שם' seems extra. רבי מנחם בר יוסי uses this extra word for cursing parents: just as cursing ה׳ needs the שם, so does cursing parents. A כינוי is not enough for the death penalty.

keyTerms.meaning: Why does the פסוק need to say this? (the word looks extra)

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows the חכמים' exemption is not just logic. It rests on a דרשה that links cursing parents to cursing ה׳.

phrases.english: It is Rabbi Menachem bar Yosei.

phrases.aramaic: דְּתַנְיָא: רַבִּי מְנַחֵם בַּר יוֹסֵי אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: As it is taught in a baraita: Rabbi Menachem bar Yosei says:
"When he curses a name, he shall be put to death"
phrases.notes: ויקרא 24:16

phrases.english: Why does the verse need to say "name"?
phrases.notes: The same פסוק already said 'ונוקב שם ה׳', so this second 'שם' looks extra.

phrases.english: It taught about one who curses his father and his mother,
that he is not liable until he curses them with the Name.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 27 by naming the תנא and bringing his source.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The חכמים are רבי מנחם בר יוסי, who learns from the extra 'שם' that cursing parents carries the death penalty only when done with the שם המיוחד.

steps.title: רבי ינאי: everyone agrees about cursing oneself or another
steps.stepSummary: On the משנה's case of cursing oneself or another person, רבי ינאי says that this is the view of everyone.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'One who curses himself or his friend, etc.' רבי ינאי said: and this is everyone's view.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה, about cursing yourself or another person, and רבי ינאי says nobody argues about it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier the חכמים needed the שם המיוחד for the death penalty when cursing ה׳ or parents. רבי ינאי says that here, for cursing oneself or another, even the חכמים agree the איסור applies with a כינוי too.

keyTerms.meaning: One who curses himself or another person

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the חכמים' leniency carries over here. For cursing oneself or another, everyone agrees there is an איסור even with a כינוי.

phrases.english: And one who curses himself or his fellow, etc.
Rabbi Yannai said: And this is everyone's view.
phrases.notes: 'Everyone' includes the חכמים, who were lenient about a כינוי in the earlier cases.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the next case in the משנה and shows that the earlier מחלוקת does not apply here.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The איסור of cursing oneself or another person with ה׳'s names, even a כינוי, is agreed upon by all.

steps.title: The source for the איסור of cursing oneself
steps.stepSummary: The איסור of cursing oneself comes from 'השמר לך ושמור נפשך מאד', and רבי אילעא's rule that 'השמר' always means a לא תעשה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Cursing oneself is forbidden, because it says: 'Only watch yourself and guard your soul very much.' This follows רבי אבין, quoting רבי אילעא, who said: wherever it says 'watch', 'lest', or 'do not', it is a negative commandment.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now gives the source for each איסור, starting with cursing oneself. It quotes a פסוק and a general rule that turns the word 'השמר' into a real prohibition.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says to guard your own soul, and cursing yourself goes against that. On its face, 'השמר' could sound like general advice. רבי אילעא's rule shows that 'השמר', 'פן', and 'אל' always make a לא תעשה, so this is a true איסור.

keyTerms.meaning: Watch yourself (a word that signals a prohibition)
And guard your soul very much

steps.whyThisMatters: רבי אילעא's rule is a general tool used across ש״ס: the words 'השמר', 'פן', and 'אל' turn a פסוק into a לא תעשה.

phrases.english: Himself — as it is written:
"Only watch yourself and guard your soul very much"
phrases.notes: דברים 4:9

phrases.aramaic: כִּדְרַבִּי אָבִין אָמַר רַבִּי אִילְעָא, דְּאָמַר:
phrases.english: In line with Rabbi Avin, who said in the name of Rabbi Ile'a, who said:
Every place where it says "watch," "lest," or "do not" —
it is nothing but a negative commandment.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the פסוק behind the first half of the rule in step 29 (cursing oneself).
steps.raayaObject: That cursing oneself is a real איסור (a לא תעשה).
steps.raayaSupportSource: The פסוק 'רק השמר לך ושמור נפשך מאד' together with רבי אילעא's rule that 'השמר' means a לא תעשה.

steps.title: The source for the איסור of cursing another person
steps.stepSummary: The איסור of cursing another person comes from the פסוק 'לא תקלל חרש'.
steps.simpleTranslation: And cursing one's fellow is forbidden, because it says: 'Do not curse a deaf person.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the source for the second half of the rule, cursing another person, from the פסוק about not cursing a deaf person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא does not need a special rule here, because 'לא תקלל' is already worded as a prohibition. It uses this פסוק as the source for cursing any other person.

keyTerms.meaning: Do not curse a deaf person

steps.whatToRemember: Cursing ה׳ or parents carries the death penalty. רבי מאיר says this applies even with a כינוי. The חכמים require the שם המיוחד; for parents, those חכמים are רבי מנחם בר יוסי (step 28). Cursing oneself or another with ה׳'s names is a plain איסור that everyone agrees to: oneself from 'השמר לך', another from 'לא תקלל חרש'.

phrases.english: And his fellow — as it is written:
"Do not curse a deaf person."
phrases.notes: ויקרא 19:14. The גמרא uses this פסוק for cursing any other person.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the sources for step 29 by giving the פסוק for cursing another person.
steps.raayaObject: That cursing another person is an איסור.

steps.title: The curse that is written in the תורה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה: saying 'יככה ה׳ אלהים' or 'יככה אלהים' is the curse written in the תורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'The Lord God shall strike you,' and likewise 'God shall strike you': this is the curse that is written in the Torah.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new line of the משנה, which says that 'God shall strike you' counts as the curse written in the תורה. This sets up the two stories that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the case of the משנה, someone uses a curse to make witnesses swear. The משנה is telling us which wording counts as the real curse found in the Torah. The גמרא quotes it here mainly because the next story is about how to say these words out loud.

keyTerms.meaning: 'God shall strike you': the curse wording

phrases.english: "The Lord God shall strike you,"
phrases.notes: These are the words of the משנה. Compare דברים 28:22.

phrases.english: and likewise "God shall strike you"
that is the curse that is written in the Torah.

steps.triggerLanguage: יַכְּךָ ה׳ אֱלֹהִים וְכֵן יַכְּכָה אֱלֹהִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the משנה after the side discussion about cursing oneself and others.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'יככה אלהים' is the curse written in the Torah.

steps.title: רב כהנא is told to say the curse politely
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא recited the משנה word for word ('God shall strike you') in front of רב יהודה, who told him: say it politely.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא sat before רב יהודה and recited this משנה exactly as it is taught. רב יהודה said to him: say it in a polite way.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story. A student said 'God shall strike you' to his teacher while quoting the משנה, and the teacher told him to change the wording.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even though he was only quoting the משנה, saying 'you' in front of his רבי sounded like he was cursing him. So רב יהודה told him to say it differently, for example 'God shall strike him.'

keyTerms.meaning: Say it politely: change the wording so it does not sound offensive
As we learned it, word for word

phrases.aramaic: יָתֵיב רַב כָּהֲנָא קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב יְהוּדָה,
phrases.english: Rav Kahana sat before Rav Yehuda,
and he sat and was saying
this mishna just as we learned it.
He said to him: Say it euphemistically.
phrases.notes: He means: don't say 'you' to your teacher. Say 'him' instead.

steps.triggerLanguage: יָתֵיב רַב כָּהֲנָא קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A story about how to say out loud the curse wording quoted in step 32.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When quoting a curse from the משנה in front of one's teacher, change the wording so it is not addressed to him.

steps.title: A student is told to say a פסוק politely
steps.stepSummary: A student recited a curse from תהלים in front of רב כהנא, and רב כהנא told him: say it politely.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain Sage sat before רב כהנא and recited: 'God will also break you forever, take you up and pluck you from the tent, and uproot you from the land of the living, Selah.' רב כהנא said to him: say it in a polite way.
steps.whatsHappening: A second, similar story: this time the curse came from a פסוק, and the teacher still told the student to change the wording.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The difference from the first story is the source. Here the curse is from תנ״ך, not the משנה. Even so, רב כהנא (the student in the first story) now tells his own student to say it politely.

keyTerms.meaning: A certain one of the Sages

phrases.english: A certain one of the Sages sat
before Rav Kahana,
and he sat and was saying:
"God will likewise break you forever;
phrases.notes: תהלים 52:7

phrases.english: He will take you up and pluck you from the tent,
and uproot you from the land of the living, Selah."
He said to him: Say it euphemistically.

steps.triggerLanguage: יָתֵיב הָהוּא מֵרַבָּנַן קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב כָּהֲנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel story to step 33, this time with a פסוק instead of a משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even when quoting a curse from a פסוק in front of one's teacher, change the wording.

steps.title: Why tell both stories?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why it needs two stories that teach the same thing.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why do I need two stories?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why both stories are needed, since they seem to teach the same lesson. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא assumes nothing is told for no reason. If both stories only teach 'say it politely,' one should be enough. So there must be something new in the second story.

phrases.english: Why do I need two?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions why both stories (steps 33 and 34) are needed.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What does the second story add beyond the first?

steps.title: Even פסוקים may be said politely
steps.stepSummary: Without the second story, we might think we may change the wording of a משנה but not of a פסוק. The second story teaches that even a פסוק may be said politely.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said: this applies only to a משנה, but with פסוקים we do not change the wording. So it teaches us that we do.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the second story is needed to teach something new: we may change the wording even when quoting a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One might think the exact words of a פסוק must never be changed, while a משנה could be adjusted. The second story shows that respect for one's teacher allows rewording even when quoting תנ״ך.

keyTerms.meaning: פסוקים, verses of the Torah or תנ״ך

steps.whatToRemember: To respect a teacher, we may reword a curse so it is not aimed at him, whether we are quoting a משנה or a פסוק.

phrases.english: Lest you say:
this applies only to a mishna,
but with verses, say that we do not employ a euphemism;
it teaches us otherwise.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 35.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The second story teaches that even פסוקים may be said politely, not only a משנה.

steps.title: A blessing that hints at a curse
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה: if one says 'God shall not strike you,' 'God shall bless you,' or 'God shall benefit you,' רבי מאיר holds him liable and חכמים exempt him.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'May God not strike you,' 'May He bless you,' 'May He do good to you': רבי מאיר holds him liable, and the חכמים exempt him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה, about adjuring witnesses with positive wording that only hints at a curse. רבי מאיר and חכמים argue about it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר learns the hidden opposite: 'may He bless you if you testify' means 'if you don't, may He not bless you.' The חכמים say this is not enough, because no curse was actually said.

keyTerms.meaning: May He do good to you

steps.confusionAlert: These sound like blessings, but the argument is whether the opposite, a hidden curse, is implied for someone who does not testify.

phrases.english: "May He not strike you," or "May He bless you,"
phrases.notes: These are the words of the משנה, said to witnesses: 'if you come and testify.'

phrases.english: or "May He benefit you"
Rabbi Meir deems him liable,
and the Rabbis deem him exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the next case in the משנה after finishing the side discussion about saying curses politely.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Positive wording that implies a curse: רבי מאיר holds him liable, חכמים exempt him.

steps.title: רבי מאיר doesn't usually infer a positive from a negative
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי מאיר's ruling in the משנה, because elsewhere he does not accept מכלל לאו אתה שומע הן.
steps.simpleTranslation: But רבי מאיר does not hold that from a negative statement you can infer a positive one!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבי מאיר's ruling in the משנה, which it just quoted. It points out that the ruling clashes with a rule רבי מאיר holds elsewhere.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'God shall not strike you' only makes the witness liable if we read into it the opposite: 'and if you don't testify, God will strike you.' That reading is מכלל לאו אתה שומע הן. But רבי מאיר is known to reject this kind of inference, so how can he hold the witness liable?

keyTerms.meaning: From a negative statement you can hear (infer) a positive one
But isn't it so that... (opens a challenge)

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two sides. רבי מאיר is the one who makes the witness liable here, yet he is also the one who usually rejects reading a 'yes' into a 'no.' That is exactly the problem.

phrases.english: But doesn't רבי מאיר not hold
that from a 'no' you can hear a 'yes'!
phrases.notes: רבי מאיר usually holds that both sides of a condition must be spelled out, so you can't infer one from the other.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי מאיר's ruling from the משנה quoted in step 37.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי מאיר's ruling that a witness is liable for 'God shall not strike you'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ruling depends on inferring a positive from a negative, which רבי מאיר rejects elsewhere.

steps.title: Reverse the opinions
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers by switching the names: the חכמים make him liable and רבי מאיר exempts him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Reverse it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by suggesting the names in the משנה got switched.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If we swap the opinions, רבי מאיר is the one who exempts the witness. That fits his view that you can't infer a positive from a negative. The חכמים would then be the ones who make him liable.

keyTerms.meaning: Reverse, meaning switch which opinion belongs to whom

phrases.english: Reverse it.
phrases.notes: Switch the names: the חכמים make him liable, and רבי מאיר exempts him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 38 by changing who said what.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי מאיר holds the witness liable, which goes against his own principle.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי מאיר exempts the witness and the חכמים hold him liable.

steps.title: רב יוסף: our version of the משנה is exact
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק taught the משנה just as we have it, so רב יוסף concludes the wording is exact and the reversal is rejected.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רבי יצחק came, he taught it the way we learned it. רב יוסף said: since we learned it this way, and רבי יצחק also taught it this way, we can conclude that our version is exact.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the 'reverse it' answer. A second, independent report of the משנה matches our version.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two separate traditions agree: ours and the one רבי יצחק brought. So רב יוסף says the names in the משנה were deliberate and should not be switched. That means the answer from step 39 falls away.

keyTerms.meaning: When he came (usually from ארץ ישראל to בבל)

phrases.english: When רבי יצחק came,
he taught it as we learned it.
רב יוסף said:
Now that we learned it this way,

phrases.aramaic: וְכִי אֲתָא רַבִּי יִצְחָק תָּנֵי הָכִי,
phrases.english: and when רבי יצחק came, he taught it this way,
conclude from it that we learned it exactly.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי אֲתָא רַבִּי יִצְחָק, תְּנָא כְּדִתְנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the reversal proposed in step 39.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The answer of switching the opinions
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Two independent traditions confirm the משנה's wording, so it can't be reversed.

steps.title: The question comes back
steps.stepSummary: With the reversal rejected, the original question about רבי מאיר is difficult again.
steps.simpleTranslation: But then it's difficult!
steps.whatsHappening: Now that switching the names is off the table, the גמרא says the challenge from step 38 is back. This line sets up the next answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר really does make the witness liable. So we are again stuck with the clash against his rule that you can't infer a positive from a negative.

keyTerms.meaning: But then it is difficult (the old question returns)

phrases.english: But then it's difficult!
phrases.notes: This brings back the question from step 38: how can רבי מאיר infer a 'yes' from a 'no'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After step 40 rejects the reversal, it brings back the challenge of step 38.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי מאיר's ruling in the משנה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Same as before: the ruling needs מכלל לאו אתה שומע הן, which he rejects.

steps.title: Money matters vs. איסור matters
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר rejects the inference only in money matters. In איסור matters he accepts it.
steps.simpleTranslation: When he doesn't hold it, that is in money matters. But in איסור matters, he does hold it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by limiting רבי מאיר's rule to money cases only.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר's demand that both sides be spelled out applies to money deals. A שבועת העדות is an איסור matter, so there he does allow inferring a 'yes' from a 'no.' That is why he holds the witness liable.

keyTerms.meaning: Matters of איסור (religious law, not money)

steps.whatToRemember: According to this answer, רבי מאיר rejects מכלל לאו אתה שומע הן only in money matters. In איסור matters, like this oath, he accepts it.

phrases.english: When he doesn't hold it, it is in money matters;
but in איסור matters he does hold it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the returning challenge of step 41.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the scope of a principle (distinction)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי מאיר never accepts inferring a positive from a negative.
steps.terutzMaskana: He rejects it only in money matters; in איסור matters he accepts it.

steps.title: But סוטה is an איסור case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins a challenge: סוטה is an איסור case, so it can test the money-vs-איסור answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: But here is סוטה, which is an איסור matter,
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new challenge to the answer it just gave. This line only sets it up; steps 44 and 45 finish the challenge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer said that in איסור matters רבי מאיר accepts inferring a positive from a negative. The גמרא now brings up סוטה, which is clearly an איסור case, to test that claim. The full attack comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: A woman suspected by her husband of being unfaithful

phrases.english: But here is סוטה, which is an איסור matter,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a challenge to the distinction made in step 42.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that רבי מאיר accepts מכלל לאו אתה שומע הן in איסור matters
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: סוטה is an איסור case, so it can test whether רבי מאיר really accepts the inference there. Steps 44 and 45 spell out the details.

steps.title: רבי תנחום בר חכינאי: the word הִנָּקִי is written
steps.stepSummary: רבי תנחום בר חכינאי explains that the guilty outcome in the סוטה verse is found inside the word הִנָּקִי.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי תנחום בר חכינאי said: "הִנָּקִי" is written.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a statement from רבי תנחום בר חכינאי about the סוטה verse. It is setting up the next move, where this statement will be used against the answer from Step 42.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The סוטה verse openly states only the good outcome: 'be clean' if she did not sin. רבי תנחום says the guilty outcome is found by reading the word הִנָּקִי in a special way. This means the verse does spell out both outcomes, but only through this unusual reading.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Be clean / be free' (במדבר 5:19), said to the סוטה if she is innocent
A wife suspected of adultery who goes through the bitter-water test

phrases.english: And Rabbi Tanchum bar Chachinai said:
"Hinnaki" is written.
phrases.notes: The word from במדבר 5:19 is read as if it also says חִנְקִי, 'be strangled'. That reading covers the guilty case.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source that the challenge begun in Step 43 needs.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The guilty outcome in the סוטה verse comes from a special reading of הִנָּקִי.

steps.title: Without הִנָּקִי, the inference would not work even for איסור
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא infers that only the special word made the סוטה case work. Without it we would not infer a positive from a negative, even in an איסור case.
steps.simpleTranslation: The reason it works is that "הִנָּקִי" is written. But if not, we do not say "from a negative you hear a positive"!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws a conclusion from רבי תנחום's statement. This conclusion goes directly against the answer from Step 42.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 42 said that רבי מאיר accepts 'from a negative you hear a positive' in איסור matters. סוטה is an איסור case, yet the verse still had to hint at the guilty outcome through הִנָּקִי. This shows that, without that hint, we would not have inferred it, so even in איסור the inference is not relied on.

keyTerms.meaning: But if it were not so
From a negative statement you can infer the positive

steps.confusionAlert: This line is not saying the סוטה law is uncertain. It is saying the verse had to spell out the guilty case through הִנָּקִי, and that is exactly what weakens the money-vs-איסור answer.
steps.whyThisMatters: It puts the answer from Step 42 back in doubt, so the גמרא will need a new way to explain רבי מאיר.

phrases.english: The reason is that "hinnaki" is written,
but if not so,
"from a negative you hear a positive"
we do not say!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses רבי תנחום's statement to complete the challenge against Step 42.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer in Step 42 that רבי מאיר accepts the inference in איסור matters
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: סוטה is an איסור case, yet the guilty outcome needed the special word הִנָּקִי. So without it, the inference would not have been made, even in איסור.
